title: Merge Sorted Streams

source.name: Original exercise; classic technique (k-way merge with a heap)

statement:
There are `k` lists of integers and each list is already sorted in non-decreasing order (a list may be empty). Imagine merging all of them into one sorted sequence. Print the first `M` values of that merged sequence, separated by spaces on one line.

**Input.** The first line holds `k` and `M`. Then follow `k` lines; each starts with the length `L` of the list, followed by its `L` values.

**Output.** The `M` smallest values of all the lists together (equal values are kept, one per occurrence), in non-decreasing order.
constraints: 1 ≤ k ≤ 20000; the total number of values N satisfies 1 ≤ N ≤ 20000 in this browser version (the idea scales to millions)
hints: Putting every value into one array and sorting it works in O(N log N). Think about doing less work when M is small, and about streams that cannot be held in memory at once.
At any moment the next value of the merged sequence is the smallest among the current heads of the k lists. A min-heap of at most k heads finds it in O(log k).
Push the first value of every non-empty list as (value, list number, position). Pop the smallest, print it, and push the next value from the same list. Stop after M pops.
editorial: The merged order is produced one value at a time. The next output is always the smallest **unconsumed head** among the lists, because each list is sorted so nothing behind a head can be smaller than the head itself. Keep the current head of every non-empty list in a min-heap together with the list number and position. Pop the minimum, output it, and push the successor from the same list if there is one. The heap never holds more than `k` entries, so every step is `O(log k)`, and `M` steps cost `O(k + M log k)` (building the heap with `k` pushes costs `O(k log k)`, or `O(k)` with heapify). Compare with concatenating and sorting everything, `O(N log N)`: the heap wins when `M` is much smaller than `N`, and it is the only approach that works when the lists are streams that do not fit in memory. In languages without a built-in priority queue (JavaScript) write the sift-up and sift-down loops yourself.

solutions.python:
import sys
import heapq

data = sys.stdin.read().split()
k, m = int(data[0]), int(data[1])
pos = 2
lists = []
for _ in range(k):
    length = int(data[pos])
    pos += 1
    lists.append(list(map(int, data[pos:pos + length])))
    pos += length
heap = [(lst[0], i, 0) for i, lst in enumerate(lists) if lst]    # (value, which list, position in it)
heapq.heapify(heap)
out = []
while heap and len(out) < m:
    value, i, j = heapq.heappop(heap)
    out.append(value)
    if j + 1 < len(lists[i]):
        heapq.heappush(heap, (lists[i][j + 1], i, j + 1))
print(" ".join(map(str, out)))
